query: Prior calculations on concentrated alloys examined variations in atomic mass and force constants, temperature-dependent lattice heat transport, or DFT-derived elastic properties coupled to analytical conductivity estimates; some estimates require a Debye temperature. The cited simulations generally represented perfect, defect-free bulk crystals. Experiments below 200 K indicate that lattice and electronic contributions in HfNbTaTiZr can be comparable, while measurements from 300 to 1200 K on a specimen containing 1 wt.% oxygen report total conductivity of 10–17 W/(K m). Available analytical approaches do not capture all relevant atomic-scale complexity in refractory high-entropy alloys, and separate transport studies do not establish a predictive solution for this alloy. Given these constraints, what testable hypothesis could an unspecified new predictive approach make for HfNbTaTiZr without conflating lattice and electronic heat transport? Explain why it should outperform earlier approaches, quantify the expected improvement, define its temperature and sample applicability limits, identify supporting observations from the cited work, and specify decisive comparisons with low- and high-temperature measurements that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: A newly developed multi‐scale predictive model that explicitly decouples lattice (phonon) and electronic heat transport—including the influence of oxygen impurities and inherent lattice distortions—will forecast the thermal conductivity of HfNbTaTiZr with significantly improved accuracy (error reduced by at least 50%) over prior analytical approaches that assume defect‐free crystals and use a single Debye temperature.
generation.material_initial_state: Refractory high-entropy alloy HfNbTaTiZr synthesized with a typical impurity level of ~1 wt.% oxygen, exhibiting inherent lattice distortions from atomic size and mass fluctuations.
generation.intervention: Employ a combined computational strategy that integrates molecular dynamics (to capture anharmonic phonon scattering from lattice distortions and oxygen defect effects) with density-functional theory calculations (to obtain electron scattering parameters) and a machine learning regression to separately predict lattice and electronic contributions.
generation.conditions: Simulations and subsequent experiments conducted over a temperature range from below 200 K (to capture the low-temperature regime where lattice and electronic contributions are comparable) up to 1200 K (typical service conditions) under controlled oxygen content and microstructural defect levels.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and oxygen-induced defect states that modulate both the force-constant fluctuations (affecting phonon scattering) and electron relaxation times.
generation.mechanism: By accurately modeling the anharmonic phonon dynamics and electron scattering processes separately, the new approach can decouple and quantify the contributions from lattice vibrations and free carriers. This decoupling avoids the conflation inherent in earlier models that treated the alloy as an ideal, defect-free crystal.
generation.predicted_outcome: The model is predicted to show that below ~200 K, lattice and electronic contributions are nearly equal, while from 300 to 1200 K the overall thermal conductivity remains in the experimentally observed range (10–17 W/(K·m)) with a reduced prediction error (≈50% improvement) compared to models based on a single Debye temperature.
generation.baseline: Earlier analytical and DFT-based approaches that assume perfect, defect-free crystals and use averaged properties (such as a single Debye temperature) to estimate conductivity in high-entropy alloys.
generation.boundary: The predictive model is expected to be valid for HfNbTaTiZr alloys with impurity levels around 1 wt.% oxygen and typical levels of lattice disorder; its accuracy may diminish for alloys with significantly different defect types or impurity concentrations.
generation.uncertainty: Quantifying the exact improvement in predictive accuracy is uncertain due to challenges in precisely determining electron-phonon coupling parameters and training data limitations for machine learning; the estimated 50% error reduction is approximate and will require rigorous experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare HfNbTaTiZr alloy samples with a controlled oxygen content (~1 wt.%) and measure the total thermal conductivity as well as the decoupled lattice and electronic contributions over a temperature range covering both regimes (<200 K and 300–1200 K). Use complementary experimental techniques such as inelastic neutron/X-ray scattering to probe phonon dynamics and terahertz spectroscopy or electrical measurements to assess electronic transport.
measurements: Electronic conductivity and derived thermal contribution at high temperatures (300–1200 K)
Total thermal conductivity across the full temperature range
Characterization of defect structure and oxygen impurity levels
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the independently measured lattice and electronic contributions deviate from the model predictions by more than ±25%, or if the overall thermal conductivity error reduction (relative to traditional models) is not at least 50%, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) provide new research avenues for alloy combinations in the periodic table, opening numerous possibilities in novel-alloy applications. However, their electrical characteristics have been relatively underexplored. The challenge in establishing an HEA electrical conductivity model lies in the changes in electronic characteristics caused by lattice distortion and complexity of nanostructures. Here we show a low-frequency electrical conductivity model for the Nb-Mo-Ta-W HEA system. The cocktail effect is found to explain trends in electrical-conductivity changes in HEAs, while the magnitude of the reduction is understood by the calculated plasma frequency, free electron density, and measured relaxation time by terahertz spectroscopy. As a result, the refractory HEA Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 thin film exhibits both high hardness and excellent conductivity. This combination of Nb15Mo35Ta15W35 makes it suitable for applications in atomic force microscopy probe coating, significantly improving their wear resistance and atomic-scale image resolution. Surprisingly, our work seems to suggest that the high entropy mixing of many elements is ineffective in terms of phonon engineering, while it can be used to effectively impact electron transport and thus the electronic contribution to thermal transport, as demonstrated by Jin et al.. Still, this result is specific to this HEA, characterized by a force-constant disorder similar to binary alloys. In order to effectively impact phonons, larger force-constants fluctuations should be sought, by choosing elements with more different characteristics. This is the case of HCP and BCC HEAs, where, however, the larger atomic differences introduce as well a stronger mass and atomic size disorder, so that the force-constant disorder does not dominate anymore.

Thermoelectric materials have attracted extensive attention because they can directly convert waste heat into electric energy. As a brand-new method of alloying, high-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted much attention in the fields of materials science and engineering. Recent researches have found that HEAs could be potentially good thermoelectric (TE) materials. In this study, special quasi-random structures (SQS) of PbSnTeSe high-entropy alloys consisting of 64 atoms have been generated. The thermoelectric transport properties of the highest-entropy PbSnTeSe-optimized structure were investigated by combining calculations from first-principles density-functional theory and on-the-fly machine learning with the semiclassical Boltzmann transport theory and Green–Kubo theory. The results demonstrate that PbSnTeSe HEA has a very low lattice thermal conductivity. The electrical conductivity, thermal electronic conductivity and Seebeck coefficient have been evaluated for both n-type and p-type doping.
